items.title: New Game Uses Local AI Model Trained Entirely on Studio's Own Artists
items.excerpt: Studio Atelico built more than 10 prototypes around a local, on-device model trained only on its own artists' work. The takeaways: authored constraints, artist consent, statistical testing, and tighter creative-technical collaboration.
items.why: A concrete answer to the consent problem: train small, train on your own art, keep inference on-device — generative art becomes a studio asset rather than a legal risk.

items.title: Nvidia tech behind PUBG's genAI team mates will let folks chat to creature-collecting RPG Aniimo's not-Pokemon next year
items.excerpt: Nvidia ACE, the tech that powered PUBG's generative AI teammates, is heading into Aniimo, where players will be able to talk to the creatures they collect from early 2027.
items.why: ACE moves from tech demo to a shipping creature-collector — the design question stops being 'can NPCs talk' and becomes 'what should a talking companion be allowed to say'.

items.title: We're finally talking about AI, ft. David 'Rez' Graham and Luke Dicken
items.excerpt: Two veteran game AI practitioners discuss AI techniques in game development — and the nature of the work itself, separating classic game AI craft from the generative hype cycle.
items.why: The people who built game AI before it was a buzzword draw the line between systems design and generative slop — useful vocabulary for any design team arguing about tools.

items.title: Rockstar formed a new LA-based team to develop more realistic NPCs for Grand Theft Auto 6
items.excerpt: Rockstar spun up a dedicated Los Angeles studio focused almost entirely on NPC design, aiming to build on the interactive fidelity of Red Dead Redemption 2.
items.why: The biggest game in the world answers 'believable NPCs' with an entire hand-built team, not a model — a pointed counterexample to the generative-NPC pitch.

items.title: Roblox makes three of its AI safety tools open source
items.excerpt: Roblox released three of its AI moderation and safety models as open source, via the Robust Open Online Safety Tools community it co-founded with Google, OpenAI, and Discord.
items.why: UGC platforms are where AI moderation is a design constraint, not a policy footnote — open models let smaller creator platforms inherit the safety layer.

items.title: The Witcher 4 dev is "still predominantly using people" over AI in development, says CEO
items.excerpt: CD Projekt Red's CEO says the studio still leans on people rather than AI for The Witcher 4, while conceding that every studio has to make its own judgment call.
items.why: A flagship RPG studio publicly setting the human/AI ratio — the clearest signal yet of where AAA craft budgets are actually going.

items.title: Video Game Companies Keep Trying To Bait And Switch Us With AI, And It Sucks
items.excerpt: 1666: Amsterdam, Blood of Dawnwalker and others insist AI assets never made the final build — but 'not in the shipped game' is not the same as AI-free production.
items.why: Disclosure language is becoming a design-process question: where in the pipeline AI touched the work is now the thing players are auditing.

items.title: Create Procedural UE5 Animations Based on Music with Vizibeat
items.excerpt: Vizibeat is an Unreal Engine plug-in that drives procedural animation directly from an audio track, producing motion without any keyframing.
items.why: Procedural, signal-driven animation is the quiet alternative to generative video — the input is the music, the output stays fully controllable in-engine.

items.title: No, the Humankind 2 announcement trailer wasn't made with gen-AI, developer Amplitude clarifies
items.excerpt: Amplitude had to publicly explain that Humankind 2's reveal trailer was hand-made after players read its look as generative AI output.
items.why: A new art-direction hazard: certain rendering choices now read as 'AI' to audiences, so studios are styling around suspicion.

items.title: 5 takeaways from Gamescom 2026: A truly global show, AI's impact, and what was missing
items.excerpt: A round-up of the trends coming out of Gamescom 2026, with AI's practical footprint across development and publishing among the headline talking points.
items.why: A show-floor read on where AI actually landed in production this year, rather than where vendors said it would.

items.title: Skillprint Flow turns gameplay into human performance data for AI
items.excerpt: Skillprint launched Flow, an API and toolset that converts the gameplay studios already produce into structured human-performance data usable for AI training and evaluation.
items.why: Reframes telemetry as a designed artifact — what you instrument in a game becomes a product, which changes how systems get designed in the first place.

items.title: Nvidia announces ray-traced Nanite, native anti-cheat, and DLSS 4.5 at Gamescom 2026
items.excerpt: Nvidia used Gamescom to detail a wave of developer-facing updates across DLSS, RTX and GeForce Now, including ray-traced Nanite and DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction.
items.why: Neural rendering keeps sliding into the art pipeline: what artists author and what the GPU infers are being redrawn again.

items.title: NVIDIA's DLSS 5: Slop Or Not?
items.excerpt: Artists and players have been running DLSS 5 across a range of games, and the results split the room on whether neural enhancement is a look or a smear.
items.why: The visual-literacy fight over neural rendering, argued with side-by-sides rather than vibes — useful for anyone defending an art direction.

items.title: DLSS 5 finally has a use case - making Cyberpunk 2077 genuinely dystopian
items.excerpt: Players pointing DLSS 5's neural filter at Cyberpunk 2077 found the uncanny smoothing weirdly appropriate for the game's world.
items.why: An accidental art-direction lesson: a filter everyone calls a defect becomes intentional when the fiction can absorb it.
